name: Descartes's Six Primitive Passions
description: René Descartes's Les passions de l'âme (The Passions of the Soul, 1649) proposes that every passion of the soul, however complex, is a combination or degree of six primitive ones: wonder (admiration), love (amour), hatred (haine), desire (désir), joy (joie), and sadness (tristesse). These six are not Paul Ekman's twentieth-century "basic emotions" wearing older dress — they predate that model by more than three centuries, arrive by a wholly different method (introspective philosophical analysis plus Descartes's own mechanistic physiology of "animal spirits" moving through the body and pineal gland), and answer a different question: not which facial expressions are cross-culturally recognized, but which passions cannot be built out of any others. Descartes wrote for a physician's and a princess's eyes (the treatise grew out of his correspondence with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia) rather than for a laboratory.

_note: Six of Descartes's derived/compound passions from Part III are now represented — esteem and contempt (art. 149-150, species of wonder), hope and its contrary crainte (art. 165-166, joy+desire mixed, and its inverse), jealousy (art. 167-169, itself built from crainte plus desire for an already-possessed good), and remords de conscience (art. 60, 177, a doubt-gated species of sadness) — chosen because this school's own founding brief named them as the clearest worked examples of Descartes's compositional method, and because together they show different depths of derivation: two-primitive blends, a three-tier chain in jealousy, and a single-primitive-plus-condition case in remords. Part III catalogues dozens more (veneration, scorn, indecision, courage, boldness, emulation, derision, envy, pity, self-satisfaction, repentance, approval, gratitude, indignation, anger, vainglory, shame, and others) — this remains a sample of the compositional method, not a catalogue, and no claim of completeness is made or should be inferred. The physiological mechanism (animal spirits, the pineal gland) is now worked through with Descartes's own case study of a frightening encounter (art. 31-36, 39) rather than only summarized; its modern scientific status is confined to that item's own Research note, per house style. Remaining gaps: Descartes's treatment of how the passions relate to virtue and the will's power over them (Part I, art. 41-50, 147-148) is not yet represented; nor is his own separate passion of peur/terreur (art. 174, 176), which he argues is not really a distinct passion at all, or repentir (art. 191), the certainty-gated counterpart to remords — the school currently has an item for crainte (hope's contrary) but not for peur, and an item for remords but not repentir. No new group item was added for the six derived-passion items: unlike the three existing groups, which each partition an explicit structural pairing Descartes himself makes among the six primitives, these six derived passions do not share one single Cartesian organizing principle, and grouping them together would imply a systematic second tier this sample does not provide.

The 1649 French text and its early translations are long out of copyright; no specific translator's wording is quoted here — every section is original prose describing Descartes's claims, not a translation excerpt.

sections.Definition: Descartes places wonder (admiration) first among the six and treats it as unique: a sudden surprise of the soul that causes it to attend to and consider objects that seem rare or extraordinary — before the soul has judged whether the object is good or bad for it. Wonder is purely cognitive orientation toward novelty; unlike the other five, Descartes says it has no bodily opposite and does not depend on whether the object benefits or harms us.
sections.Why it comes first: Because wonder precedes any judgment of good or evil, Descartes treats it as the passion that makes the other five possible — nothing can become an object of love, hatred, desire, joy, or sadness until it has first been noticed as significant. Excess wonder, in his account, produces astonishment (étonnement), which can freeze a person into inaction; its useful degree he calls generosity of curiosity, a disposition to keep learning.
sections.Research note: This is the clearest point of contrast with basic-emotion models built around universal facial expressions (see the ekman-basic school in this collection): Descartes's wonder is defined by its relationship to prior knowledge (is this new to me?), not by any claimed facial signature.

sections.Definition: Descartes defines love as an agitation of the soul caused by the animal spirits, which impels the soul to join itself willingly to objects that appear agreeable to it — a felt movement toward union with something judged good, whether that something is a person, an object, or an idea.
sections.Its degrees: Descartes distinguishes affection (for something judged inferior to oneself), friendship (for an equal), and devotion (for something judged superior — God, one's country, one's sovereign). He treats these as differences of the same primitive passion rather than as separate ones.
sections.Research note: Descartes explicitly pairs love with hatred as its bodily and functional opposite (both concern union versus separation from an object), which is why they are grouped together in this deck's second-level composite.

sections.Definition: Hatred, in Descartes's scheme, is the mirror of love: an agitation caused by the spirits that impels the soul to will itself separated from objects presented to it as harmful. Where love draws the soul toward union, hatred drives it toward distance and rejection.
sections.Its physiology: Descartes ties hatred's bodily signature to a supposed bitterness in the blood and a tightening around the heart, part of his broader (and now superseded) mechanistic account of how each passion moves the animal spirits differently through the body.
sections.Research note: Descartes's specific physiology — animal spirits, the pineal gland as the soul's seat — is not treated as a live scientific claim by this school; his primitive-passion taxonomy is read independently of the 17th-century mechanics used to explain it.

metadata.image_credit: "Hatred or Jealousy", plate 20 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Desire is an agitation of the soul, caused by the spirits, that disposes it to will for the future whatever it represents to itself as agreeable — the only one of the six primitive passions Descartes defines as inherently future-facing.
sections.Its scope: Descartes treats desire broadly: it covers wanting to obtain a good one does not yet have and wanting to avoid an evil one fears, and even the desire to preserve a good one already possesses (since preservation is itself a kind of future-directed willing). He does not give desire a named opposite among the six.
sections.Research note: Descartes's desire is closer to what later philosophy calls a conative or motivational state than to a discrete felt emotion — it is defined by what it moves the soul to will, not primarily by how it feels.

metadata.image_credit: "Desire", plate 8 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Joy is an agreeable emotion of the soul, in which the enjoyment it possesses consists — the felt experience of having, right now, what one has judged to be good. Where desire looks forward and love reaches toward union, joy registers a good already present or already attained.
sections.Its relation to love: Descartes treats joy as frequently accompanying love (one is glad about what one loves) but keeps them conceptually distinct: love is the movement toward union, joy is the register of possession. One can, on his account, love something one does not yet possess, in which case joy is absent and desire dominates instead.
sections.Research note: Descartes pairs joy with sadness as its direct opposite — both concern a good or evil the soul takes to be already present, rather than merely possible.

metadata.image_credit: "Laughter", plate 10 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access). Used for joy (Le Brun's plate is titled by its outward expression, laughter, rather than by Descartes's own term).

sections.Definition: Sadness is a disagreeable languor in which the soul's discomfort consists, arising from an evil, or a lack, that the soul represents to itself as belonging to it now — the counterpart to joy's registration of a present good, this time registering a present evil or absence.
sections.Its relation to hatred: As joy relates to love, sadness relates to hatred: hatred is the movement of rejection toward a harmful object, sadness is the felt discomfort of the evil or lack already being present. Descartes treats prolonged, ungrounded sadness as physiologically corrosive, and recommends attending to genuine present goods as a corrective — an early version of what later therapeutic traditions would call reappraisal.
sections.Research note: Descartes's six close on an opposing pair (joy/sadness) that mirrors the earlier pair (love/hatred), leaving wonder and desire as the two primitives without a named opposite in his own scheme.

metadata.image_credit: "Sadness", plate 13 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Esteem opens Descartes's catalogue of derived passions in Part III of the treatise. Esteem, regarded as a passion, is "the soul's inclination to represent to itself [an object's] value," caused by a movement of the spirits that strengthens the brain's impressions relating to that value (art. 149). Contempt is its mirror, covered in the same article: the soul's inclination to consider an object's baseness or insignificance. Article 54, Descartes's own summary from Part II, glosses self-directed esteem as "esteem (with generosity or pride)."
sections.Built from wonder, not from love: Descartes is explicit that esteem and contempt are not fresh primitives but two species of the very first one, wonder: we esteem or contemn an object by wondering at its greatness or its insignificance (art. 150). He adds a precise qualification: esteem is often aroused by love, and contempt by hatred, but "this isn't universal" — that affective route holds only in the special case where the inclination to weigh an object's greatness already comes from having more or less affection for it. Wonder, not love, is esteem's structural parent.
sections.Self-esteem and generosity: When esteem and contempt turn on the self, Descartes gives them an explicit composition (art. 160). Self-esteem felt as vanity, or as the virtue he calls generosity (générosité), is "aroused by a movement composed of the movements of wonder, joy, and love" — three movements, not four — self-love, plus love for whatever occasions the good opinion. Its contrary, humility (virtuous or unvirtuous), is "composed of the movements of wonder, sadness, and self-love mingled with hatred" for one's own faults. Generous self-esteem — knowing that only the free use of one's will truly belongs to oneself, and resolving to use it well — is what Descartes calls "a kind of key to all the other virtues and a general remedy for every disorder of the passions" (art. 161).
sections.Research note: No other school currently in this library uses "esteem" as a cross-grammar key, so no matching decision was needed here. Worth flagging for a future integrator: Aquinas's eleven passions (schools/aquinas-passions) have no analogue to Cartesian wonder at all — admiratio is not one of his eleven — so that scholastic scheme has no wonder-species slot for a self-evaluative passion of this kind. Descartes's admission of wonder as an irreducible primitive is what makes esteem and contempt possible as a distinct category in his system in the first place.

sections.Definition: Contempt (mépris), Descartes's mirror to esteem, is "the soul's inclination to consider the baseness or insignificance of the object it contemns," caused by a movement of the spirits that strengthens the brain's impression of that insignificance (art. 149). Descartes notes that, ordinarily, "esteem" and "contempt" name only opinions about worth, with no passion involved — they become passions specifically when a movement of the animal spirits accompanies the judgment.
sections.Built from wonder, sometimes joined to h: Like esteem, contempt is a species of wonder (art. 150) — a felt reaction to how small an object seems, prior to any question of whether the low opinion is deserved. Contempt is often aroused by hatred, Descartes adds, but again "isn't universal": the affective case is a special instance, not contempt's structural definition. Article 54 glosses self-directed contempt as "contempt (with humility or abjectness)" — see this deck's "estime" item for the fuller compositional account of that self-directed case (wonder, sadness, and self-love mingled with hatred for one's own faults, art. 160).
sections.Two related states Descartes names but d: Two further Part III articles extend contempt's family without giving it a new primary name. Veneration (art. 162) is esteem directed at a free cause capable of doing us good or harm, mixed with an anxious wish for its approval. Scorn (art. 163) is contempt for such a free cause, judged too far beneath us to help or harm us — composed, Descartes says explicitly, of the movement that produces wonder together with the movement that produces confidence or boldness.
sections.Research note: "Contempt" already appears as an emotion_key in ekman-basic, plutchik-wheel (its disgust+anger dyad), and the generated across-the-schools aggregate; it is reused here because the everyday concept — looking down on something as beneath notice — is genuinely shared. But the underlying mechanisms diverge enough to withhold a cross-link: Plutchik's contempt is explicitly hostile ("rejection fused with hostility," in that school's own gloss), while Descartes's mépris is not — at root it is a dispassionate judgment of insignificance, arising from wonder rather than from anger or disgust, with hatred only ever a contingent accompaniment. No cross-link is proposed between this item and Plutchik's for that reason; the shared English word covers two structurally different accounts of what contempt is.

sections.Definition: Hope is "a disposition of the soul to be convinced that what it desires will happen" (art. 165) — one of several derived passions for which Descartes states the compositional recipe outright: hope "is caused by a particular movement of the spirits, namely the movements of joy and of desire mixed together." Its contrary in the same article, which he calls crainte (see this deck's separate "crainte" item), is the disposition convincing the soul that what it desires will not happen; the two, he notes, can occur together, since a person can hold reasons on both sides of the same desired outcome at once.
sections.The extremes: confidence and despair: Article 166 continues the same thought. When hope grows so strong that it entirely drives out crainte, it changes its nature and is called confidence or assurance — desire itself quiets, because the outcome now feels certain rather than merely awaited. When crainte instead drives out all hope, it becomes despair, which Descartes says extinguishes desire altogether, because despair represents the desired thing as impossible, and desire, on his account, applies only to what is still possible — a condition he states in articles 58 and 145 and restates inside article 166 itself.
sections.Research note: No other school in this library currently keys an item "hope," so no cross-school matching decision was needed here. Worth flagging for a future integrator rather than silently linking: Aquinas's spes (schools/aquinas-passions) is deliberately kept transliterated in that grammar rather than keyed "hope," precisely because spes gates on arduousness — a future good must be difficult to attain before Aquinas will call the appetite's movement toward it spes at all. Descartes's espérance carries no such gate; it needs only that the desired thing be believed possible, whether attaining it is easy or hard. The two are built from different premises about what makes a passion count as this one, so no cross-link to spes is proposed.

sections.Definition: Crainte is the disposition of the soul convincing it that a desired outcome will not happen (art. 165) — the direct contrary of hope, built on the same underlying desire read under an unfavorable estimate of the odds. Descartes states hope's own spirit-composition explicitly (joy and desire mixed); he does not give crainte's composition with that same explicitness in article 165 — he treats it there, and again in article 166, as hope's opposite pole rather than defining a separate spirits-movement for it in its own right.
sections.Not Descartes's only passion translated: This is one of two Cartesian passions that English translations of this treatise render "fear," and they are not the same passion. The crainte of article 165 is the future-facing negative partner of hope, gated only on desire and an unfavorable estimate of possibility. A second, harsher passion — peur or terreur, opposed to boldness rather than to hope (art. 174) — concerns a near evil that resists escape rather than a merely doubted future outcome; Descartes goes further and denies peur is even a distinct passion at all, calling it (art. 176) "merely an excess of shrinking reluctance, wonder and anxiety [crainte]." This item covers crainte only (art. 58, 165–166); the school does not yet have a separate item for peur/terreur (art. 174, 176).
sections.Research note: Keyed "fear" to match this library's existing precedent of using one plain-English key across structurally different technical "fear" concepts — see greek-pathe, where Aristotle's rhetorical phobos and the Stoics' ethical phobos are both keyed "fear" despite naming different projects, with the difference stated in each item's own Research note rather than resolved by transliteration. The alternative of keying this item "crainte" would avoid any risk of confusion with Descartes's own peur, but would break with that established cross-school pattern for a case that is, if anything, less divergent than the Aristotle/Stoic pair. No cross-link to aquinas-passions' timor is proposed: timor is gated on arduousness (a future evil hard to escape) in a way crainte is not, so the two concepts diverge in the same way spes and espérance do (see the "esperance" item).

sections.Definition: Jealousy is, in Descartes's own words, "a kind of anxiety [crainte] having to do with our desire to keep possession of some good" (art. 167) — a third-tier derivation: desire for a good already possessed, read through crainte, which is itself built from that same desire plus an unfavorable estimate of the odds (see this deck's "crainte" item). Descartes treats one diagnostic as central: jealousy tracks the esteem in which the good is held more than the objective strength of the reasons to doubt keeping it — "it results less from the strength of the reasons that make us think we may lose the good, as from the high esteem in which we hold it," which is why it seizes on the slightest grounds for doubt and inflates them.
sections.Honorable and blameworthy cases: Articles 168–169 give Descartes's own worked contrast, useful for showing the passion is not condemned outright. A captain jealous of an important fortress, or a woman jealous of her honour, are jealous rightly, on his account, because the good genuinely at stake is great. A miser's jealousy over his hoard, or a husband's jealousy of his wife, he treats as contemptible — in the latter case because true love, on his analysis, carries no inclination to distrust; what the jealous husband actually loves, Descartes argues, is not the person but "the good he imagines to consist in his having sole possession of her."
sections.Research note: No cross-link is proposed. "Jealousy" otherwise appears in this library only in thought-forms (Besant and Leadbeater's 1901 theosophical colour-and-shape key for auras, identifying a plate rather than analysing a passion) and in the generated across-the-schools aggregate, which draws on that same entry. Neither is a real conceptual peer for Descartes's structured, multi-tier account of jealousy as fear for a possessed good.

sections.Definition: Remords de conscience is "a kind of sadness that comes from our doubt about whether something we are doing or have done is good" (art. 177). Descartes treats the doubt as the passion's defining feature, not an incidental cause: if we were certain an ongoing action was bad we would not be doing it, since the will (on his account) is drawn only toward what has some semblance of goodness; if we were certain a past action was bad, the resulting sadness would be repentance (repentir, art. 191) instead, a different, more bitter passion. Remords's function, he holds, is to prompt inquiry into the doubtful action and to inhibit repeating it until the doubt resolves.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"rem: Ordinary English "remorse" names sadness or guilt over a wrong one is already convinced one has committed. Descartes's remords is narrower and points the other way: it requires uncertainty, and dissolves into a different passion (repentir) the moment that uncertainty resolves into conviction of wrongdoing. This is not an idiosyncratic reading of the French: the standard modern English edition of this treatise (Jonathan Bennett's translation, cross-checked here against the French Wikisource text for every article cited) flags the same gap in its own glossary, noting that articles 60 and 177 both show remords "essentially involves uncertainty about whether one has acted wrongly, which our 'remorse' doesn't." Keying this item plain "remorse" would silently import the certainty Descartes's own definition excludes.
sections.Research note: plutchik-wheel already uses "remorse" as an emotion_key (its sadness+disgust dyad, glossed there as blended grief and self-disgust). That gloss reads closer to what Descartes calls repentir than to remords: Plutchik's dyad presumes the bad deed is already acknowledged, not doubted. No cross-link is proposed between this item and Plutchik's remorse for that reason. Should this school later add an item for Descartes's repentir (art. 191), that would be the closer candidate for comparison with Plutchik's dyad.

items.name: Animal Spirits and the Pineal Gland — the Physiological Mechanism

sections.The apparatus: Descartes's mechanism rests on two moving parts. Animal spirits are, on his account, simply the finest and fastest-moving parts of the blood — "merely bodies... except for being extremely small and moving very fast" (art. 10) — sifted out by the heart's heat and channeled into the brain's cavities, from which they flow into the nerves (hollow fibre-bundles, art. 12) and on into the muscles, producing movement whenever more spirits arrive at one muscle of an opposed pair than at the other (art. 11). The pineal gland is the second part: a small, unpaired gland deep in the brain that Descartes argues is the soul's one point of direct contact with the body (art. 31).
sections.Why a gland, and why this one: Descartes's argument for the gland (art. 32) turns on symmetry. The eyes, ears, hands, and most of the brain itself come in pairs, yet a person has one unified perception of one object at a time. Somewhere, he reasons, the two channels of sense-information must be combined into a single impression before reaching the soul — and only this one small, unpaired gland fits that requirement. He explicitly rejects the heart as the passions' true seat (art. 33): the heart only feels involved because a nerve runs from brain to heart, in the same way pain is felt "in the foot" by means of nerves in the foot, without the soul doing any of its work there.
sections.Worked through: seeing something frighte: Descartes supplies his own case study (art. 35–36). Light from an approaching animal forms two retinal images, one per eye; these produce two further images on the brain via the optic nerves; spirits carry both images toward the pineal gland, where corresponding points of the two images converge onto the same points of the gland, fusing into one image that "acts directly on the soul and makes it see the shape of the animal." If that shape resembles something that has hurt the body before, this arouses anxiety, then either boldness or fear/terror, depending on the body's state, the soul's habitual strength, and past experience of fighting or fleeing similar threats. Spirits from the gland are then routed partly to the leg-nerves (for flight) and partly to nerves that constrict or expand the heart's openings, in a way that keeps blood moving so as to maintain and strengthen the fear already begun — which is also why, Descartes notes, the passion is felt "chiefly as if it were in the heart," even though, per article 33, the heart is not where the soul is actually doing anything at all.
sections.The same stimulus, different outcomes: Descartes adds (art. 39) that the identical gland-movement that produces fear in one person can produce courage in another, because brains are wired differently: in some people the spirits from that same gland-state flow instead toward the hand-muscles (for defense) and toward nerves that drive blood to the heart in the pattern needed to sustain fighting rather than fleeing. Habituation and training, on his account (art. 50), can rewire which gland-movement follows which stimulus — his own illustration is the difference between a gun-shy dog and one trained to run toward the sound of a shot.
sections.Research note: Descartes's mechanism was largely superseded within a generation of his own century. The pineal gland (epiphysis cerebri) is now understood as an endocrine structure that produces melatonin, with no established role as a singular mind-body interface; "animal spirits" as fine, fast-moving blood particles have no counterpart in the modern physiology of the nervous system, which instead describes electrochemical signaling along neurons. What is worth preserving from the mechanism, independent of its specific physiology, is the structural claim it was built to support: that a single, non-bilateral point is where sensory streams converge into unified experience, and that habituation can rewire which bodily response follows a given perception (art. 39, 50) — a structural intuition later, unrelated neuroscience would revisit by very different routes and very different evidence.

items.name: Wonder — the Passion Without an Opposite

sections.Definition: Descartes treats wonder as structurally singular among the six: it has no bodily opposite, does not depend on the object's being judged good or bad, and functions as the gateway passion that makes the other five possible by first flagging an object as significant.

items.name: Love and Hatred — Union and Separation

sections.Definition: The pair Descartes builds around the soul's movement toward or away from an object it has judged good or harmful — union (love) against separation (hatred).

items.name: Desire, Joy, and Sadness — Future and Present

sections.Definition: Desire looks toward a future good or the avoidance of a future evil; joy and sadness register a good or evil the soul takes to already be present. Descartes treats these three as temporally distinct readings of the same underlying appraisal — good/evil, future/present.

items.name: Derived Passions — Built From the Six

sections.Definition: Descartes holds that only six passions are primitive and that every other is composed of them, so the derived passions are a second tier in his own scheme rather than a category imposed on it. These six are a sample of the dozens Part III works through — chosen because each shows the composition clearly — and not the set. Where a passion is built from particular primitives, its item says which.

items.name: Les Passions de l'Âme — the Six Primitives

sections.Definition: Descartes's 1649 treatise argues that every passion the soul can feel, however complex or culturally particular, reduces to six primitives — wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy, sadness — and their combinations. He arrives at the six through introspective philosophical analysis paired with his own mechanistic physiology (the animal spirits, the pineal gland as the point of contact between soul and body), not through cross-cultural observation or facial measurement.
sections.Not Ekman's six, three centuries earlier: It is tempting to read Descartes's primitives as an early sketch of Paul Ekman's twentieth-century basic-emotion list (see the ekman-basic school in this collection), since both name a small closed set. They are not the same list (Descartes has wonder and love where Ekman has disgust and surprise, and neither list maps onto the other one-to-one), and they are not reached the same way: Ekman's rests on cross-cultural facial-recognition experiments conducted from the 1960s onward; Descartes's rests on 17th-century rationalist introspection and mechanistic physiology. The resemblance is in the ambition — a small, non-reducible set — not in the method or the content.
sections.Research note: Descartes's physiological mechanism (animal spirits circulating through nerves, the pineal gland as the soul's seat) was superseded by later neuroscience within his own century and is not treated here as a live empirical claim. What survives as philosophically live is the classificatory question itself — how many primitive passions are there, and by what test does a passion count as primitive rather than compound — a question later basic-emotion theories inherit without crediting Descartes as their source.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial — Recursive Repatterning's own commentary, not a claim Descartes made.* Descartes's method (introspection plus a single thinker's physiological theory) cannot establish that these six are universal or biologically fixed, only that they were, to him, conceptually irreducible. A constructionist account would treat even that irreducibility claim as itself a product of 17th-century French rationalist categories rather than a discovery about the human soul in general — a caution worth holding for any small, closed list, this one included.

metadata.evidence_note: Descartes reached his six primitives by philosophical introspection combined with a since-superseded mechanistic physiology, not by empirical measurement of any kind. No cross-cultural or experimental evidence was collected or claimed; the taxonomy stands or falls as philosophical argument, not as a scientific finding.
